data.title: Broken Access Control on Administrative Functionality
data.summary:
Administrative functionality was reachable by standard users because access
control was applied only in the user interface rather than enforced on the
requests themselves.
data.description:
The application presented different interface elements according to the
authenticated user's role, concealing administrative functionality from standard
users. The underlying endpoints, however, performed no role check of their own
and processed any authenticated request they received.

Because the interface is rendered by the client, its behaviour is under the
control of the user. An attacker who knows or discovers the address of an
administrative endpoint can issue the request directly, and the application
executes it. Endpoint addresses are commonly disclosed in client-side code,
predictable from naming conventions, or present in documentation.

The same weakness applied to role assignment itself, where the value determining a
user's privileges was accepted from the request rather than read from the
authenticated session, allowing a user to grant themselves elevated access.

No exploitation is involved. The attacker issues ordinary, well-formed requests
that the application is not entitled to accept, which makes the activity
difficult to distinguish from legitimate administrative use in application logs.
data.impact:
A standard authenticated user could perform administrative actions within the
application, including the management of other users' accounts and access to data
across the full user base. Where role assignment could be influenced, the user
could grant themselves persistent administrative access, and the resulting
activity would appear legitimate in the application's own audit records.
data.recommendation:
1. Enforce authorisation on the server for every request, verifying the
   authenticated user's role against the operation requested. Interface-level
   concealment is a usability measure and provides no security.

2. Implement the check centrally, applying it by default to all endpoints and
   requiring an explicit exemption for those intended to be public, so that new
   functionality is protected without further action.

3. Derive the user's role from the authenticated session on the server. Never
   accept role, permission, or identity values from the request.

4. Deny by default, so that an endpoint with no explicit authorisation rule
   rejects requests rather than accepting them.

5. Log all administrative actions with the identity of the user performing them,
   and alert on administrative operations performed by accounts not assigned that
   role.

6. Test each endpoint with a request issued by a standard user as part of the
   development process, rather than relying on the interface to demonstrate that
   access is restricted.
